message.content:
You are a security auditor on an authorized penetration test of "Nxeon," a VPS/game-server hosting business (a Hostinger-style clone). The codebase is a Next.js 15 App Router + TypeScript + Prisma + Postgres app at /opt/nxeon on a live Proxmox host. This is the OWNER's own infrastructure and this audit is fully authorized.

CONTEXT — why this audit exists: the host was just root-compromised. An attacker sent `POST /` (a Next.js Server Action invocation, which returned HTTP 303) and ~5 seconds later a root-owned cryptominer appeared on disk. The web app runs as the unprivileged user `nxeon`; a separate worker process runs as ROOT. The exact vulnerable handler was never proven. Your audit is the primary means of finding it.

YOUR MISSION — audit the Server Action authorization surface. In Next.js App Router, EVERY exported async function in a file with the `"use server"` directive is a remotely-invokable HTTP endpoint (invoked by POSTing a Next-Action header; the action ID is derivable from the client bundle, so treat all of them as publicly reachable by an attacker who read the JS). This is exactly the class of bug that likely caused the incident.

For every `"use server"` module under /opt/nxeon/lib and /opt/nxeon/app (find them with: grep -rl '"use server"' /opt/nxeon/lib /opt/nxeon/app --include=*.ts --include=*.tsx), enumerate every exported async function and classify each:
1. **Auth gate**: Does it call an auth guard (requireUser / requireAdmin / realUser / currentUser-with-check / equivalent) BEFORE any side effect? Flag any exported action with NO auth check, or where the check comes after a side effect.
2. **IDOR / ownership**: If it accepts an id, userId, serverId, etc. as a parameter, does it verify the caller OWNS that object before acting? Flag actions that trust a caller-supplied id without an ownership check.
3. **Dangerous capability**: Does it enqueue a job (db.job.create), write/read/delete files, run a command, mint credentials, touch billing/wallet, or modify infra? These are the high-value targets — an unauthenticated or IDOR-able one of these is critical.

Pay special attention to any action whose name or body suggests it could lead to code execution, file writes to sensitive paths, or job creation that the root worker later executes. Also specifically check lib/actions-board.ts's runCardStageAction (it spawns scripts) and anything that enqueues PROVISION / CLAUDE_BUILD / GAME_CONFIG / MIGRATE jobs.

CONSTRAINTS: READ-ONLY. Do not edit any file, do not run builds, do not restart services, do not run `npm install`. Other Claude sessions and audits are running on this same box concurrently — touch nothing, only read. Reading files and grepping is fine.

OUTPUT: A findings list, most-severe first. For each: file:line, the function name, the specific gap (missing auth / IDOR / dangerous sink with no guard), a concrete one-sentence exploit scenario (what an unauthenticated attacker could do), and a severity (critical/high/medium/low). Then a short section naming your top 3 suspects for the incident's actual entry vector and why. Be concrete and cite file:line for everything. Aim for a thorough but readable report — prioritize real, exploitable findings over style nits.

Trigger especially when the user references a spreadsheet file by name or path — even casually (like "the xlsx in my downloads") — and wants something done to it or produced from it. Also trigger for cleaning or restructuring messy tabular data files (malformed rows, misplaced headers, junk data) into proper spreadsheets. The deliverable must be a spreadsheet file. Do NOT trigger when the primary deliverable is a Word document, HTML report, standalone Python script, database pipeline, or Google Sheets API integration, even if tabular data is involved.
- design: Create a design canvas - a multi-artboard visual design published as an Artifact that runs Claude Design's canvas editor (an early preview of Claude Design inside Claude Code). You DRAFT the design as .dc.html artboards laid out on one pan/zoom canvas; where saving is enabled for the user's account they refine every element visually (click-to-select, a properties panel, inline text editing, undo/redo) and Save publishes a new version for everyone, otherwise they get a view-and-export (PNG/PDF) preview of your draft. Good for UI mockups and screen flows, landing pages, marketing and social graphics, and print pieces - posters, flyers, brochures as single-page artboards; memos and reports as one flowing artboard. Use when someone wants a design, mockup, wireframe, UI or screen design, landing page, poster, flyer, brochure, banner, card, one-pager, or any visual layout they would rather tweak by hand than in code. Only for CREATING or re-seeding a canvas; an existing one is edited in its published Artifact.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. When the destination is a first-party document connector (host-designated, never self-described) that renders live charts, hand it the rows (inline, or as an uploaded data file the chart cites) rather than a rendered PNG/SVG — a picture of a chart loses hover, data inspection and per-value comments. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts. - Load before writing any artifact, including a skill-instructed Markdown one - Markdown is never a shortcut past the design pass.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts - when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, remembering what people do on it (a poll, a sign-up sheet, a checklist, a document edited in place — it saves new versions of itself), keeping state shared across viewers, knowing who is viewing, asking Claude a question of its own, storing files people add, or handing the viewer a file to save. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever any such runtime behavior would make an artifact more useful, before writing the page.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review. For ultra on a GitHub.com PR target, --post asks to post the finished review’s findings to the PR as a single comment from the user’s GitHub account (not a review; the launch dialog still confirms in interactive sessions, while non-interactive mode posts on the flag alone) and --no-post hides that option.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.

Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").

TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).

#!/usr/bin/env python3
import os, re, subprocess, sys

files = subprocess.check_output(
    ['grep','-rl','"use server"','/opt/nxeon/lib','/opt/nxeon/app',
     '--include=*.ts','--include=*.tsx']).decode().split()
files = [f for f in files if f.strip()]

AUTH = re.compile(r'\b(requireUser|requireAdmin|requireStaff|requireArea|realUser|currentUser|requireOrg|assertNotImpersonating|requireArea|getSessionUser|requireTeam|requireCustomer|requireApiUser|requirePartner|assertTeamAccess|assertOwn|requireOwner)\b')
# side effects that indicate the action "does something"
SINK = re.compile(r'\b(db|prisma|tx)\.\w+\.(create|update|updateMany|delete|deleteMany|upsert|createMany)|\.job\.create|spawn\(|exec\(|execSync|writeFile|fs\.(rm|write|mkdir|unlink|open|appendFile)|revalidatePath|redirect\(|cookies\(\)|sshExec|runCommand')

def funcs(src):
    out=[]
    # export async function NAME(
    for m in re.finditer(r'^export\s+async\s+function\s+(\w+)\s*\(', src, re.M):
        out.append((m.group(1), m.start()))
    # export const NAME = async (
    for m in re.finditer(r'^export\s+const\s+(\w+)\s*=\s*async\s*(?:function)?\s*\(', src, re.M):
        out.append((m.group(1), m.start()))
    # export async function* / etc ignore
    return sorted(out, key=lambda x:x[1])

report=[]
for f in sorted(files):
    try:
        src=open(f, encoding='utf-8', errors='replace').read()
    except Exception as e:
        continue
    fs_=funcs(src)
    if not fs_: continue
    # compute body spans
    lines_start = {}
    for i,(name,pos) in enumerate(fs_):
        end = fs_[i+1][1] if i+1 < len(fs_) else len(src)
        body = src[pos:end]
        lineno = src[:pos].count('\n')+1
        has_auth = bool(AUTH.search(body))
        # position of first auth vs first sink
        auth_m = AUTH.search(body)
        sink_m = SINK.search(body)
        auth_at = auth_m.start() if auth_m else 10**9
        sink_at = sink_m.start() if sink_m else 10**9
        auth_before_sink = auth_at < sink_at
        report.append((f, lineno, name, has_auth, auth_before_sink, sink_m.group(0) if sink_m else '', ))

# Print files/functions with NO auth guard at all
print("=== EXPORTED ACTIONS WITH NO AUTH GUARD ANYWHERE IN BODY ===")
for f,ln,name,has_auth,abs_,sink in report:
    if not has_auth:
        print(f"{f}:{ln}\t{name}\tSINK={sink}")

print()

---

# Nxeon Server Action Authorization Audit — Findings

## Scope & method
Enumerated every true `"use server"` module by checking that the directive is the *actual first statement* (not merely the phrase appearing in a comment). Result: **exactly 110 action modules**, all under `/opt/nxeon/lib/actions-*.ts`, `/opt/nxeon/lib/actions.ts`, `/opt/nxeon/lib/hosting-email.ts`, `/opt/nxeon/app/admin/promotions/actions.ts`, `/opt/nxeon/app/riddle/actions.ts`. No inline server actions exist in any `.tsx` page/component, and none live outside `lib`/`app`. I ran a static triage for every exported async function reaching a dangerous sink (`db.job.create`, `hostingTask.create`, `spawn`/`exec`, `writeFile`/SFTP, credential mint, wallet), then hand-verified the special-attention targets and used four sub-agents to verify IDOR/ownership across ~45 sink-bearing functions. Auth model confirmed in `/opt/nxeon/lib/auth.ts`, `/opt/nxeon/lib/rbac.ts`, `/opt/nxeon/lib/staff-grants.ts`.

## Headline result
**The Server Action authorization surface is robust and consistent. I found no missing-auth, no IDOR, no privilege-escalation, and no unguarded dangerous-capability server action.** Every dangerous sink is gated by `requireUser`/`requireAdmin`/`requireStaff`/`requireArea`/`requireGrant` plus a local ownership helper (`ownedServer`/`ownedVolume`/`loadOwned`/`ownedTargetServer` — all of the form `if (x.userId !== user.id && user.role !== "ADMIN") throw`), money paths add `assertNotImpersonating`, and job/worker payloads carry only validated ids or allowlisted/type-coerced values. This code has visibly been through prior hardening (dense comments referencing fixed IDOR/impersonation/CAS bugs).

The specific items the task called out all check out:
- `lib/actions-board.ts:506 runCardStageAction` — `requireAdmin()` first; commands come from a fixed `STAGE_ACTIONS` allowlist (`node`/`bash` on 4 hardcoded scripts); the only interpolated value (git commit msg) is passed via env var, expanded inside double quotes. **OK.**
- CLAUDE_BUILD (`lib/actions-claude.ts:30/113`) — `requireUser` + `server.findFirst({id, userId})` ownership + approval compare-and-swap + BYOK gate. **OK.**
- GAME_CONFIG (`lib/actions-game-config.ts:84`) — `ownedServer` + schema-validated config; payload is `{serverId}` only. **OK.**
- MIGRATE (`lib/actions-migrate.ts:559`) — `ownedTargetServer` + SSRF `vettedSourceHost` + DNS-rebind defense + every option field coerced with `=== true` "so nothing else can ride in"; payload is `{migrationId}`. **OK.**
- PROVISION (order.ts / game-order.ts / actions.ts / actions-nxcloud.ts / actions-server-lifecycle.ts) — all `requireUser` + own-server; admin-grant path is `requireAdmin`. **OK.**

## Findings (all low/informational — none is the incident vector)

**F1 — LOW / latent-hardening. Privileged helper modules embed the literal phrase `"use server"` in their header comments.**
`lib/ssh-exec.ts`, `lib/sftp.ts`, `lib/game-control.ts`, `lib/hosting-db.ts`, `lib/free-minecraft-control.ts`, `lib/cpanel-inline.ts`, `lib/freemc-capacity.ts`, `lib/mailcow.ts`, `lib/order.ts`, `lib/stripe-cards.ts` (and others). These export raw, unauthenticated primitives — `sftp.ts:384 writeFileText(server,path,content)`, `ssh-exec.ts:192 withServerSsh`, `hosting-db.ts:134 runScopedSql`, `game-control.ts:648 runRcon`. They are currently safe because the directive is commented out, not active (verified: the first real statement is an `import`, so Next does not register them). Gap: if any future edit or refactor promotes one of these to a real `"use server"` file, every one of these SSH/exec/SQL/file-write helpers becomes a directly-invokable, un-authenticated endpoint with attacker-supplied arguments — instant RCE. Exploit scenario (latent): an unauthenticated `POST` to a promoted `writeFileText` action writes arbitrary files to any server over SSH. Recommendation: remove the phrase from these comments (rephrase to "not a client-callable action module") so it can never be mistaken for/refactored into a directive.

**F2 — INFO. Two customer wallet-adjacent actions omit `assertNotImpersonating`** (`lib/actions-gift.ts:108 redeemGiftCode`, `lib/actions-payment-method.ts:130 settleOutstanding`), unlike every debit path. Neither debits a wallet (one credits the caller's own balance, one mints a checkout link for the server owner), so there is no cross-account effect — consistency nit only.

**F3 — INFO / design. Shared-host blast radius.** `lib/actions-free-minecraft.ts` and the `actions-freemc-*` files gate correctly (every function resolves the server via `findUnique({where:{userId: user.id}})`, so there is no forgeable id and no IDOR), but they all SSH **as root to one shared `freemc-host`**, scoped only by the `mc-free-<userId>` container name and `shellQuote`. Correct as written; noted because any future quoting/allowlist slip there is a shared-host compromise, not a single-tenant one.

**F4 — INFO. Intended cross-tenant admin reach.** `lib/actions-files.ts` `ownedServer` (and the hosting SFTP layer) let any `ADMIN` read/write any customer's filesystem. By design, but it is real cross-tenant root-FS access behind the admin role.

## Top 3 suspects for the incident's actual entry vector

The git history is the tell: `db23182 ops(firewall): block the 2026-09-06 miner source and its pool egress` and `186e938 harden(node-agent): refuse to start on a weak token or bad port, and reject type-confused fields`.

1. **`/opt/nxeon/node-agent/index.js` — type-confusion RCE + weak-token acceptance (strongest suspect; already patched).** This is a **root HTTP service on each node**. Pre-patch it validated every JSON-body field with a bare `RegExp.test()`, which coerces: `CHAIN_RE.test(123)` passes and hands a non-string into an `execFile("iptables", […])` argv (`index.js:111 iptables()`, `:205/:213` rule paths, `:75 isStr` is the fix). The companion fix treats an agent token `< 20 chars` as absent. So an attacker who could reach the node-agent's port with a guessable/short Bearer token could push a type-confused field into a root `execFile` — a clean match for "root-owned miner ~5s later." Crucially, **this is not a `"use server"` action** and is not reachable by feeding a non-string through any action (I confirmed the app→worker→agent path is fully typed: port-forward uses `z.coerce.number()/z.enum`, snippet filenames are `nxeon-<vmid>.yaml`, no action writes raw/`JSON.parse`/spread data into a job payload). That explains why "the exact vulnerable handler was never proven" from the app side.

2. **The non-`"use server"` HTTP surface (`app/api/*` route handlers + webhooks) — not covered by this audit and the better fit for `POST /`.** A server-action `POST` returning 303 is just Next's normal redirect response and does not pin down an action; an attacker can target any action ID from `/`. Since every dangerous action is authorization-clean, an unauthenticated entry is more likely a route handler or a provisioning/payment webhook that trusts its body. These POST-able endpoints (chat, files, board attachments, terminal websocket auth, webhooks) were out of scope here and should be audited next. (The one I spot-checked, `app/api/terminal/token/route.ts`, is correctly guarded: `requireUser` + ownership + RUNNING + rate-limit.)

3. **The CLAUDE_BUILD → root-worker SSH-exec chain (`lib/actions-claude.ts`) — the highest-capability action, worth the strictest ongoing scrutiny.** It converts an AI-generated plan into arbitrary shell executed over SSH. It is owner-gated + approval-CAS-gated + BYOK-key-gated and runs on the customer's **own** VM (not the host), so it does not explain a host miner — but it is the single most dangerous server action by capability and the closest server-action analogue to the incident, so any weakening of its approval gate would be critical.

**Bottom line:** within the audited surface (Server Actions), the authorization model is sound and is very unlikely to be the entry vector. The evidence points to the **node-agent root HTTP service** (type-confusion + weak token, both already patched) as the actual root-RCE primitive, with the un-audited `app/api/*` handler surface as the most probable initial reachability. I recommend those two surfaces as the immediate next audit targets.
